title: Best Microservices Testing Tools for Kubernetes in 2026
summary: Microservices and Kubernetes testing tools for 2026 in two layers: test automation such as Testkube, Pact and k6, and environment platforms such as Signadot and Release.
body_markdown:
The best microservices testing tools for Kubernetes come in two layers. Test automation tools such as Testkube, Pact, Playwright and k6 write and run the tests, and environment platforms such as Signadot, Release, Bunnyshell and Okteto give each change somewhere real to run them.


Most teams need one or two tools for each type of test and one environment platform, and the environment is where most microservices test suites go wrong. Postman, Pact and Playwright all assume the services they call are running, current, and not shared with someone else’s half-finished change, which a single staging cluster stops guaranteeing past a few teams. Coding agents raise the stakes. In CircleCI’s 2026 data,[throughput grew 59 percent in a year and about 30 percent of merge attempts failed](https://www.signadot.com/blog/circleci-2026-report-agent-validation-gap/) .


This article lists the Kubernetes testing tools in each layer, what each is for, and where they overlap, checked against each vendor’s own docs and release pages on October 11, 2026. For how these tools fit a full strategy, from unit tests to production, see the[complete guide to microservices testing](https://www.signadot.com/the-complete-guide-to-microservices-testing-from-local-development-to-production/) . For why to run tests on Kubernetes rather than on CI runners, which tests need a cluster, and the test environment options side by side, see the[complete guide to Kubernetes testing](https://www.signadot.com/kubernetes-testing/) .


## Microservices testing tools for Kubernetes at a glance


There is no single best microservices testing solution, and the best tools for testing microservices depend on which layer is failing you. The table lists the tools to test microservices that teams most often combine, grouped by layer.


Microservices testing tools for Kubernetes, October 2026. Checked against each vendor's own docs on October 11, 2026. Products change quickly, so follow the links for current details. Tool What it does Where it runs Best fit


Environment platforms: somewhere real for each change to run


[Signadot](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/sandbox) Ephemeral environments that duplicate only what a change needs and share the rest of one cluster, with Jobs, Smart Tests and Plans to run tests in them An operator in your cluster, with a thin SaaS control plane PR environments and coding agents for dozens to hundreds of services, with databases, queues and Temporal


[Release](https://docs.release.com/guides-and-examples/advanced-guides/microservices-architecture) Every service of the application in one namespace per environment, with production-like data from snapshots Your AWS or GCP account, run by Release Full-stack previews of applications small enough to copy


[Bunnyshell](https://documentation.bunnyshell.com/docs/how-bunnyshell-works) A clone of a primary environment per pull request, one namespace each Your Kubernetes cluster, managed from Bunnyshell's SaaS Full-stack PR environments from Compose, Helm or Terraform


[Okteto](https://www.okteto.com/docs/previews) A namespace per developer or pull request, a full copy by default, with Divert to borrow services from a shared namespace Your own cluster Development containers and previews on your own cluster


[Qovery](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment) A deployment platform that clones a blueprint environment per pull request Your cloud account Teams that want deployment and previews in one product


[vCluster](https://www.vcluster.com/docs/vcluster/) A virtual cluster per environment, on shared nodes Your cluster Changes that need their own Kubernetes API


Test automation and orchestration: what to test and how it runs


[Testkube](https://testkube.io/) Runs existing suites as Test Workflows inside the cluster and collects the results. Does not create environments Open source runner in your cluster. Control plane as SaaS, or on premises on Enterprise One place to run and report every test type in Kubernetes


[Postman](https://www.postman.com/) API design and testing, with collections that run from CI SaaS, with a CLI API checks on each service


[WireMock](https://wiremock.org/) Simulates HTTP APIs so a service can be tested without its dependencies Open source library or server. WireMock Cloud is hosted Unit and component tests, third-party APIs


[Microcks](https://microcks.io/) Open source API mocking and testing, a CNCF Incubating project Self-hosted Shared API mocks across teams


[Pact](https://docs.pact.io/) Code-first contract tests for HTTP and message integrations Open source libraries. PactFlow, now Swagger Contract Testing, is the hosted broker Teams that own both sides of an API


[Specmatic](https://specmatic.io/) Turns API specifications into executable contracts Open source core, with commercial tools Spec-first teams


[Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) Browser automation for testing, scripting and AI agents Open source, from Microsoft End-to-end tests of web flows


[Cypress](https://www.cypress.io/) End-to-end and component tests for web apps Open source app. Cypress Cloud is paid JavaScript frontends


[Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/) WebDriver browser automation in many languages Open source Cross-browser suites in existing languages


[Shiplight](https://www.shiplight.ai/) Agents exercise UI changes in a real browser and keep the flows as Playwright-compatible E2E tests Commercial, with a free plan Browser coverage in coding-agent workflows


[k6](https://grafana.com/oss/k6/) Scripted load tests from Grafana Labs Open source CLI, the k6 Operator in your cluster, or Grafana Cloud k6 Load tests in CI and in the cluster


[Apache JMeter](https://jmeter.apache.org/) Load and performance tests across many protocols Open source Protocol-heavy load tests


[Gatling](https://gatling.io/) Load tests written as code Open source Community Edition. Gatling Enterprise is commercial Load tests kept next to application code


[OpenText Performance Engineering](https://blogs.opentext.com/what-happened-to-loadrunner-the-future-of-performance-engineering-at-opentext/) The LoadRunner family, renamed in October 2025 Commercial, on premises or cloud Enterprise performance engineering


Local development: connect a laptop to the cluster


[mirrord](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/) Runs a local process in the context of a cluster. Paid tiers add queue splitting, database branching and preview environments Open source CLI, with an operator in your cluster on paid tiers Debugging one service against real traffic


[Telepresence](https://www.telepresence.io/) Intercepts cluster traffic to a process on your laptop Open source, a CNCF Sandbox project Local development against a shared cluster


## What makes testing microservices in Kubernetes different


Testing microservices in Kubernetes is harder than testing one application because the thing under test is a graph of services, each deployed on its own schedule, and the cluster around them is part of what can break. Four problems decide which tools you need:


- **Environment provisioning.** Every change needs somewhere realistic and isolated to run, and one shared staging cluster turns into a queue once several teams deploy to it.
- **Service dependencies.** A service under test calls others. Mocking them is fast but drifts from reality, and running all of them for every change is slow and expensive.
- **Data and async flows.** Databases, Kafka or SQS queues and workflow engines such as Temporal carry state between services, and tests that share them collide.
- **Observability.** When a test fails across ten services, tracing has to point at the one that changed.


Test automation tools address none of the first three on their own. That is the job of the environment layer.


## Test automation tools vs environment platforms


The two layers answer different questions. A test automation tool decides what to test and how the tests run and report. An environment platform decides where a change runs, against which versions of its dependencies, and isolated from which other changes. Buying two tools from one layer does not fill the other: Testkube and Postman together still need an environment to point at, and an environment platform still needs tests.


The confusion is understandable, because both layers run inside the cluster and both show up under Kubernetes testing tools. They meet at test execution. Testkube runs suites in the cluster against an environment you provide, and Signadot runs suites in an environment it provides. The[complete guide’s section on the two layers](https://www.signadot.com/the-complete-guide-to-microservices-testing-from-local-development-to-production/#test-automation-tools-vs-environment-platforms) covers the overlap in more depth.


## Environment platforms for microservices testing


Environment platforms differ most in how much of the system they copy for each change. Most copy the whole environment, a namespace or a cluster per pull request. Signadot duplicates only what a change needs and plugs it into one shared environment. That choice sets spin-up time, cost as environments multiply, and how databases and queues are handled, and the[ephemeral environment tools comparison](https://www.signadot.com/guide-to-ephemeral-environments-kubernetes/#ephemeral-environment-tools-compared) lines the platforms up on all three.


### Signadot


[Signadot](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/sandbox) gives each change an ephemeral environment, called a Sandbox, that duplicates only the services and resources the change needs and plugs them into one shared environment. It links the two in three ways: it routes requests by key for synchronous traffic, routes messages by the same key for async consumers and Temporal workers, and rewrites a forked service’s configuration so it uses a new version of a dependency. Sandboxes start in seconds, and hundreds can share one cluster.


Data and dependencies are where it differs most from the full-copy platforms. A change can share the stable database with its data kept apart, or get a temporary database or a Neon or Xata branch through[resource plugins](https://www.signadot.com/docs/reference/resource-plugins) , which also provision managed queues, buckets and other cloud resources beyond the cluster and remove them when the Sandbox ends. Message routing works on one shared Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub or NATS broker, and the routing key travels through[Temporal workflows](https://www.signadot.com/docs/tutorials/testing-temporal-workers) .


Signadot also runs tests inside its environments. Jobs run existing suites in the cluster, Smart Tests compare a Sandbox’s API behavior with the stable version’s, and Plans let coding agents build test workflows. Agents connect through an[MCP server](https://www.signadot.com/docs/integrations/mcp) and[agent skills](https://www.signadot.com/docs/integrations/coding-agents/agent-skills) . Most of Signadot runs in your cluster. By default its SaaS control plane receives only resource metadata, such as workload names, namespaces, image references and status, and never source code, image contents or application data, as its[data and integrations page](https://www.signadot.com/docs/guides/admin/security/data-integrations) describes. Signadot is SOC 2 Type II.


It fits applications with dozens to hundreds of services, PR environments for every change, and coding agents that each need their own environment.


### Release


[Release](https://release.com/) , formerly ReleaseHub, is the closest direct alternative to Signadot for PR environments, built the opposite way. It puts[every service of the application in one namespace per environment](https://docs.release.com/guides-and-examples/advanced-guides/microservices-architecture) , in your AWS or GCP account, and runs those clusters for you.[Instant Datasets](https://docs.release.com/reference-documentation/instant-datasets-aws) give each environment a ready RDS, Aurora or Cloud SQL copy from a production snapshot, its Neon integration branches a database per environment, and a Terraform runner creates other cloud resources. Release now offers the same full-stack copy to AI agents through an API and an[MCP server](https://release.com/product/mcp-server) . It does not run your tests. Your CI creates the environment,[runs the suite against it](https://docs.release.com/reference-documentation/e2e-testing) and tears it down.


Release fits applications small enough to copy in full, where a standalone copy per pull request with production-like data is worth what it costs.[Signadot vs Release](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/release/) compares the two in detail.


### Bunnyshell


[Bunnyshell](https://documentation.bunnyshell.com/docs/how-bunnyshell-works) creates a clone of a primary environment for each pull request, each in its own namespace, from Docker Compose, Helm or Terraform definitions. Databases run as containers seeded from dumps, as RDS instances restored from snapshots through Terraform, or as Neon, PlanetScale or Xata branches, and queues run inside each environment. It is[billed per active environment minute](https://www.bunnyshell.com/pricing/) , and by[its own description](https://www.bunnyshell.com/e2e-testing/) it is the environment layer underneath a test runner rather than a runner itself. It fits teams that want full-stack PR environments without building the automation themselves.


### Okteto


[Okteto](https://www.okteto.com/docs/previews) gives each developer or pull request a namespace, by default with a full copy of the application.[Divert](https://www.okteto.com/docs/core/divert) lets a namespace hold only the services you changed and borrow the rest from a shared namespace, but it is opt-in, routes requests by an HTTP header, and leaves queue isolation to your own consumer code. Okteto is[billed per seat](https://www.okteto.com/docs/admin/billing) , and its free Starter plan covers five seats, self-hosted.[Okteto alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/okteto/) compares it with Signadot.


### Qovery, Northflank and other full-copy platforms


[Qovery](https://www.qovery.com/docs/configuration/environment) and[Northflank](https://northflank.com/docs/v1/application/release/pipeline/set-up-a-preview-environment) are deployment platforms with preview environments built in. Qovery clones a blueprint environment into your cloud account for each pull request, in[about three minutes by its own figure](https://www.qovery.com/solutions/ephemeral-environments) . Northflank creates a preview from a template, self-contained or sharing services and a database with a development environment.[Shipyard](https://docs.shipyard.build/) , which builds full-stack environments from Docker Compose, was[acquired by StackGen](https://stackgen.com/blog/shipyard-joins-stackgen) in September 2026.[Qovery alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/qovery/) covers the first of these in detail.


### vCluster and in-house namespaces


Platform teams often build the full copy themselves. An[Argo CD ApplicationSet](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/applicationset/Generators-Pull-Request/) with the pull request generator deploys a namespace per pull request, and[vCluster](https://www.vcluster.com/docs/vcluster/) gives each environment a virtual cluster with its own API server on shared nodes, which suits changes to CRDs or cluster-level configuration. Both copy the whole application into each environment.[vCluster alternatives](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/vcluster/) explains when a virtual cluster per pull request is worth it.


## Microservices test automation and orchestration tools


### Kubernetes test orchestration: Testkube and Signadot Jobs


When people search for a Kubernetes testing framework, or a k8s testing framework, they usually mean a way to run their existing tests inside the cluster rather than a new way to write them.[Testkube](https://testkube.io/) is the best-known tool for that. It runs suites from Postman, k6, JMeter, Playwright, Cypress, pytest, Maven, Gradle and others as Test Workflows in your cluster, triggers them from CI or cluster events, and collects logs and artifacts in one place. The runner is open source. The dashboard, multi-cluster runs, reporting, and its AI agents and MCP server need the commercial control plane, which starts at[$700 a month per runner on the Pro plan](https://testkube.io/pricing) .


Testkube does not create the environment the tests run against. Its[ephemeral environments guide](https://docs.testkube.io/articles/ephemeral-environments) starts by provisioning a namespace or cluster with “the tool of your choice”, then installs a runner into it.


Signadot’s[Jobs](https://www.signadot.com/docs/concepts/smart-tests-and-jobs) overlap with this from the environment side. They run a suite in any framework in pre-warmed pods in your cluster, in the context of a Sandbox, stream the output to CI and keep the artifacts. Smart Tests, built on Jobs, compare a Sandbox’s API responses with the stable version’s, and[Plans](https://www.signadot.com/docs/reference/plans/spec) are compiled graphs of test actions that a coding agent can author and run against any Sandbox. Teams already on Testkube keep it and point its runs at a Sandbox with the Sandbox’s routing key. Teams without an orchestrator can start with Jobs.


The other meaning of Kubernetes testing framework is a framework for testing Kubernetes itself. The Kubernetes SIGs[e2e-framework](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/e2e-framework) is a Go framework for end-to-end tests of components running in a cluster, for teams building Kubernetes components rather than applications on top of them.


### API and integration testing tools


Integration testing microservices on Kubernetes takes an API test tool and a decision about what the service calls during the test: the real dependency, or a stand-in.[Postman](https://www.postman.com/) covers API design and testing, with collections a team shares and runs from CI against each service. For testing a service without its dependencies,[WireMock](https://wiremock.org/) and[MockServer](https://www.mock-server.com/) simulate HTTP APIs. Both are open source under Apache 2.0 and actively maintained, and WireMock Cloud is the hosted version.[Microcks](https://microcks.io/) , a[CNCF Incubating project since May 2026](https://www.cncf.io/projects/microcks/) , runs API mocking and testing as a shared service.


Mocks earn their place at the unit and component layers, and for outside APIs a test cannot reach. They are the wrong tool for checking integration between your own services, because a mock keeps passing after the real service changes. The[article on mocks that pass while staging breaks](https://www.signadot.com/articles/integration-tests-pass-but-staging-breaks/) explains the failure.


### Contract testing tools


[Pact](https://docs.pact.io/) is the open source standard for consumer-driven contract tests, covering HTTP and message integrations. SmartBear’s[PactFlow](https://pactflow.io/) , now being renamed Swagger Contract Testing, is the hosted broker and adds bi-directional contract testing.[Specmatic](https://specmatic.io/) turns OpenAPI and other API specifications into executable contracts, for teams that design APIs spec-first.


Contract tests check the shape of a conversation between services, not the behavior behind it, which is why they sit next to integration tests rather than replacing them. The[complete guide to contract testing](https://www.signadot.com/contract-testing/) compares the tools in depth.


### End-to-end testing tools


End-to-end tests verify complete user journeys across services. They are the slowest and most brittle layer, so keep the suite thin.


- **Playwright:** Microsoft’s open source browser automation for testing, scripting and AI agents. Its MCP server and CLI let coding agents drive a real browser.
- **Cypress:** Open source end-to-end and component testing for web apps, with the paid Cypress Cloud on top. It suits teams whose frontends are written in JavaScript.
- **Selenium:** The long-standing WebDriver standard for browser automation, with bindings for many languages. Suites written against it tend to need more maintenance as the UI changes.
- **[Shiplight](https://www.shiplight.ai/) :** Shiplight adds a browser layer to coding-agent workflows. It gives an agent a real browser to exercise UI changes during development, then turns those flows into readable, self-healing E2E tests that live in the team’s repository. The tests are Playwright-compatible and run locally or in CI, so browser coverage stays close to the code while still running against Kubernetes-based preview, staging, and test environments. Coverage is limited to browser-facing flows, so it sits alongside API, contract, and service-level testing in a microservices stack.


### Performance and Kubernetes load testing tools


These are the performance testing tools for microservices that most teams shortlist, and all four run as Kubernetes load testing tools, either inside the cluster or against it. Load tests need the most production-like environment of any layer, because a test against an undersized or shared copy measures the copy.


- **k6:**[Grafana k6](https://grafana.com/oss/k6/) writes load tests in JavaScript, runs them from the CLI or CI, and runs distributed tests inside a cluster through the[k6 Operator](https://github.com/grafana/k6-operator) . The open source tool is AGPL-3.0, and Grafana Cloud k6 is the hosted service.
- **Apache JMeter:**[JMeter](https://jmeter.apache.org/) covers HTTP and many other protocols and runs in CI. Its most recent release is 5.6.3, from January 2024.
- **Gatling:**[Gatling](https://gatling.io/) defines load tests as code. Its Community Edition is open source and meant for local use, and Gatling Enterprise is the commercial version.
- **OpenText Performance Engineering:** the LoadRunner family,[renamed by OpenText in October 2025](https://blogs.opentext.com/what-happened-to-loadrunner-the-future-of-performance-engineering-at-opentext/) . It remains the enterprise option for teams that need its protocol coverage and vendor support.


## Local development tools: mirrord and Telepresence


Local development tools connect a process on a laptop to a cluster, so one service can be run and debugged against real neighbors without deploying it. They are not environment platforms, though the line has moved.[mirrord](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/) from MetalBear is open source for individual use. Its Team plan, at[$50 per seat a month](https://metalbear.com/mirrord/pricing/) , adds a shared cluster, queue splitting and database branching, and its Enterprise plan adds preview environments and use in CI.[Telepresence](https://www.telepresence.io/) , which started at Ambassador and is now a CNCF Sandbox project, intercepts cluster traffic to a local process. Ambassador was[acquired by Gravitee in 2025](https://www.gravitee.io/blog/ambassador-labs-gravitee-what-our-acquisition-means-for-you) .[Signadot vs mirrord](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/mirrord/) and[Signadot vs Telepresence](https://www.signadot.com/comparison/telepresence/) compare both with PR environments.


## How to choose Kubernetes testing tools for microservices


Start from where your failures come from, not from a feature list. Five questions settle most of the choice.


1. **Where do your bugs come from?** If production incidents cluster at the seams between services, the gap is in the environment layer, not in test authoring, and another test framework will not close it.
2. **How many services and teams do you have?** A system of fewer than ten services owned by one or two teams can live with a shared staging cluster or a full copy per pull request. Past that, copying everything per change gets slow and expensive, and sharing one environment while isolating each change scales better.
3. **What do your services depend on?** Ask every environment platform how it handles your databases, Kafka or SQS, workflow engines such as Temporal, and cloud resources outside the cluster. This is where platforms differ most.
4. **Who runs the tests?** CI, an orchestrator such as Testkube, the environment platform’s own runner, or a coding agent. Pick one place where results land.
5. **Where does it have to run?** In your cluster, in your cloud account, or as SaaS, and what data leaves your network. Check each vendor’s security documentation rather than its marketing page.


A Kubernetes testing framework that answers all five usually turns out to be two or three tools, not one.


## What coding agents change about microservices testing tools


Coding agents turn testing tools from something a person runs before review into something software calls many times per change.[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview) ,[Cursor](https://cursor.com/) , Codex and[GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot) now open pull requests without a person at the keyboard, and[the agent PR flood](https://www.signadot.com/blog/the-agent-pr-flood-is-here-if-you-run-istio-youre-halfway-to-solving-it/) shows what that does to test infrastructure: a 50-engineer team’s staging was sized for 100 to 150 pull requests a day, and agent output arrives as a spike it was never built to drain.


Three things follow for tool choice. Agents need an environment per run, created and destroyed through a CLI, an API or an MCP server, because an agent iterating on a failure cannot queue for staging between attempts. The tests have to run before human review, so integration and end-to-end results arrive with the pull request rather than after approval. And every environment needs a time-to-live and a cost tied to the services each change touches, not to how many agents are running, because abandoned agent runs pile up.


Both layers are adapting. Playwright ships an MCP server so agents can drive a browser, Testkube sells AI agents and an MCP server on its commercial plans, and Shiplight turns agent browser sessions into E2E tests. Most environment platforms now court agents too:[Release](https://release.com/product/mcp-server) ,[Qovery](https://www.qovery.com/docs/copilot/mcp-server) and[Shipyard](https://docs.shipyard.build/mcp) ship MCP servers, and[Bunnyshell](https://www.bunnyshell.com/claude-code-skill/) ,[Okteto](https://www.okteto.com/docs/agentic) and[Northflank](https://northflank.com/docs/v1/application/ai-agents/agent-skills) publish skills for coding agents, though most still give each agent a full copy of the environment. Signadot exposes Sandbox creation and test runs to agents through its MCP server and skills, and Plans let an agent assemble a test workflow it can run again on the next change. The[guide to validating AI-generated code](https://www.signadot.com/validate-ai-generated-code-kubernetes/) walks through the full loop.


## Where to go next


If your tests are fine and the environment is the problem, start with the[staging environments guide](https://www.signadot.com/staging-environments/) and the ephemeral environment comparison above. If you are building a strategy from scratch, the complete guide to microservices testing walks through each layer of the pyramid. If coding agents open your pull requests, start with the validation guide above, because the pipeline you build for them becomes the one everyone else uses.


## Frequently asked questions


What are the best microservices testing tools for Kubernetes?


It takes tools from two layers. For test automation, teams combine Postman for API tests, Pact or Specmatic for contracts, Playwright or Cypress end to end, k6 or JMeter for load, and Testkube to run suites in the cluster. For environments, a platform such as Signadot, Release, Bunnyshell or Okteto gives each change somewhere real to run them. The environment decides whether the results mean anything.


Is Testkube an environment platform?


No. Testkube is test orchestration: it runs existing suites, such as Postman, k6, Playwright or pytest, inside a Kubernetes cluster and collects the results. Its docs leave provisioning the environment to another tool. Environment platforms such as Signadot or Release create the environment a change runs in. The two overlap at test execution, since Signadot Jobs also run suites in the cluster.


What is a Kubernetes testing framework?


Usually a way to run tests inside or against a Kubernetes cluster rather than a new way to write them. Testkube runs existing suites as cluster workloads, and the k6 Operator does the same for load tests. The Kubernetes SIGs e2e-framework is different: a Go framework for testing components that run in Kubernetes. For microservices, any of them still needs the services under test running at current versions.


Do I need an environment platform in addition to testing tools?


Past a few teams, usually yes. Testing tools assume a stable, current environment to run against, and one shared staging cluster stops providing that once several teams deploy to it. An environment platform gives each change its own isolated environment with current dependencies, so the rest of the toolchain produces results you can trust. Small systems can manage with a shared staging environment.


Which testing tools handle Kafka, databases and Temporal?


Test frameworks call the services, so what matters is how the environment handles their dependencies. Full-copy platforms such as Release and Bunnyshell run a database and queues inside each environment. Signadot shares one broker and routes messages by key, carries the key through Temporal workflows, and gives schema changes their own database or branch through resource plugins. mirrord's paid tiers add queue splitting and database branching.


What are the alternatives to Signadot for PR environments?


Release is the closest direct alternative: it also creates an environment for every pull request, but copies the whole application into each one, in your cloud account. Bunnyshell, Okteto and Qovery copy the whole environment too, and mirrord's Enterprise plan adds preview environments of changed services. Signadot duplicates only what a change needs and shares the rest of one cluster, which suits apps with many services.


Can coding agents use these testing tools?


Yes, and most tools now expose something for agents. Playwright ships an MCP server for driving a browser, Testkube offers an MCP server on paid plans, and Signadot gives agents such as Claude Code and Cursor an MCP server and skills to create an isolated environment, run tests in it and tear it down. What agents need most is an environment per run, created without waiting on a person.


What are the best load testing tools for microservices on Kubernetes?


k6, Apache JMeter, Gatling and OpenText Performance Engineering, formerly LoadRunner, cover most needs. k6 writes tests in JavaScript and runs distributed tests in a cluster through the k6 Operator. JMeter covers the widest range of protocols. Gatling defines tests as code. Whichever you pick, run it against an environment sized and configured like production, or the test measures the environment instead of the service.
